How it works

One Link in four steps.

This is an intended pre-release workflow, not proof that every step ran merely because this page or an app was opened. Behavior, local identity storage, backups, transport, and recovery depend on the exact client build and its versioned tests.

1. Open the app.

This is an intended pre-release workflow, not proof that every step ran merely because this page or an app was opened. Behavior, local identity storage, backups, transport, and recovery depend on the exact client build and its versioned tests.

2. Pair with someone.

Installed clients are designed to pair two devices by QR plus a user-compared five-word SAS. The website runs both roles in one tab as a primitive self-test; it does not scan a camera, pair a phone, test transport, or guarantee a five-second completion time.

3. Send something.

Implemented encrypted transfers prefer a direct peer path. When direct transport is unavailable, rendezvous or relay infrastructure may carry ciphertext and observe connection, timing, routing, and size metadata.

4. Done.

The recipient receives a copy. Sender storage, endpoint backups, and encrypted relay buffers depend on the selected transport, client configuration, delivery state, and retention policy.

If they are offline

The network waits.

Buffered relay delivery is a design target and varies by build. A relay can be unable to decrypt content while still observing routing identifiers, timing, sizes, and connection metadata; retention and failover require release-specific evidence.

Encrypted before it left.

A capable relay carries ciphertext plus the routing information needed to forward it. End-to-end encryption protects content when correctly implemented, but does not hide all metadata or eliminate relay compromise risk.

Held briefly.

Do not assume a universal seven-day policy. Retention, deletion, retries, and delivery guarantees must be published and tested for the exact relay and client release in use.

Many relays, never one.

Volunteer relay discovery and automatic failover remain deployment-dependent. Availability is not guaranteed merely because the protocol permits other operators.

Staying current

Experimental update check; publisher authentication pending.

Frozen desktop bundles disable automatic and in-place installation at the runtime boundary. An update check can report availability from a mutable GitHub channel, but replacing the installed bundle remains an explicit user or operator action. Current rolling artifacts are not signed or reproducibly verified.

Experimental update check; publisher authentication pending.

A manually obtained replacement must be rejected when its SHA-256 differs from the expected value. A checksum from the same mutable channel can detect corruption but does not prove who produced the bytes; no authenticated rolling-update signature is published today.

Frozen bundles do not install updates.

The hardened frozen desktop runtime has no automatic, silent, or in-place install path. Update status may be displayed, but no Settings toggle can turn an authenticated auto-installer on because that capability is unavailable.

Replacement stays explicit.

A user or operator must obtain and replace a frozen bundle explicitly. ONE_LINK_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTOINSTALL is a legacy name retained in source history, not evidence that a frozen bundle can update itself.

If you want to hide your trail

Tap one toggle. Three hops.

Three-hop private routing is an integration target, not the path used by current website traffic. It can limit what any one relay sees, but endpoints, first and last hops, infrastructure providers, and timing observers can still infer metadata.

// roadmap pseudocode; not the current website route
// you tap "private"
pick three healthy relays
wrap message in three layers
layer 1  only the first relay can peel
layer 2  only the second relay can peel
layer 3  only the destination can read

send  no single hop sees both ends
The math if you want it

Everything else is on this page.

The implementation and primitive names are open for review. No external firm has published an audit of the daemon, protocol, or website; local demos are not an audit.

The full cryptographic stack
Website current
Local WASM buttons exercise named primitives in one browser tab. They are self-tests, not a daemon, transport, deployment, or external audit.
Worker session endpoint
/api/session advertises an ephemeral X25519 public key while ML-KEM-768 is null. The browser performs no ECDH or ML-KEM exchange with the Worker and derives no shared session key.
Daemon/protocol design
Ratchets, chunk AEAD, SAS pairing, onion routing, threshold recovery, capabilities, routing, and at-rest wrapping require versioned integration and adversarial tests. Listing a crate or primitive does not prove every path uses it.
Roadmap
Post-quantum network handshakes, multi-hop routing, universal forward secrecy, and always-on at-rest protection remain capability requirements unless a pinned release and acceptance evidence say otherwise.
